title: How The FBI Set The Trap For John Dillinger At The Biograph Theater
sources: FBI.gov History, Famous Cases & Criminals: John Dillinger
FBI Records: The Vault - John Dillinger
Wikipedia: John Dillinger; Biograph Theater; Ana Cumpanas; Little Bohemia Lodge; Melvin Purvis; Crime Control Act 1934
Hedged in script: wooden gun origin (Dillinger's own claim), the reach for a pistol (agents' account), Sage's promise (disputed)

beats.text: A hot summer night in Chicago. A movie lets out, and a crowd spills onto Lincoln Avenue.
In that crowd is the most wanted man in America. And a team of federal agents is waiting for him.
One of them holds an unlit cigar. When he lights it, the manhunt ends.
This is John Dillinger. He is thirty-one years old, and he has just watched his last film.
To understand how the trap was set, we have to go back four months, to a jail they called escape-proof.

v.q: Old Lake County Jail Crown Point

beats.text: Crown Point, Indiana. March 1934.
Dillinger is waiting for trial for the murder of a police officer, shot during a bank robbery in East Chicago.
Reporters crowd into the jail. In one famous photo, he leans on the prosecutor's shoulder and grins.
The sheriff, Lillian Holley, is sure this prisoner is going nowhere.
On the morning of March third, Dillinger pulls a pistol on a guard.
The pistol is fake. Dillinger later claimed he carved it from wood and blackened it with shoe polish.
He locks guards into cells, grabs two real machine guns, and walks out.
Then he takes the sheriff's own Ford and drives west, toward Illinois.
That one decision changes everything. Driving a stolen car across a state line is a federal crime.
Now he belongs to a small Justice Department agency called the Bureau of Investigation.

v.alt: United States Department of Justice building

beats.text: Its director is a thirty-nine-year-old named J. Edgar Hoover, and he wants this case badly.
But his agents have a problem. In early 1934, their power to make arrests and carry guns is very limited.
Dillinger, meanwhile, rejoins his gang and keeps robbing banks across the Midwest.
He has done this before. Paroled in 1933 after more than eight years in prison, he robbed bank after bank that summer.
Arrested in Ohio, he was broken out of the Lima jail by his friends, and the sheriff there was killed.
Then in Tucson, a hotel fire gave the gang away. Firefighters recognised two of them from a detective magazine.
Every time he is caught, he slips away. So the Bureau needs more than luck.
April 1934. A tip arrives. The gang is hiding at a resort lodge in the woods of northern Wisconsin.
The lodge is called Little Bohemia. Agents fly in and race toward it in borrowed cars at night.
Then the dogs start barking.
Three men leave the lodge in a car. The agents think they are gangsters and open fire.
They are not. They are local workers. One of them, Eugene Boisoneau, is killed.
In the chaos, Dillinger and his men climb out of the back windows and vanish into the trees.
Nearby, the gangster Baby Face Nelson shoots three lawmen. Agent W. Carter Baum dies.
For the Bureau, it is a disaster. Newspapers mock them. Some call for Hoover to go.
But Washington reacts. In May and June 1934, Congress passes new federal crime laws.
Robbing a national bank becomes a federal crime. And federal agents can now carry guns and make arrests.
Hoover puts one man at the centre of the Chicago hunt. His name is Melvin Purvis.
And by Dillinger's thirty-first birthday in June, the papers have a new name for him: Public Enemy Number One.
The government offers ten thousand dollars for his capture, and five thousand for information.
Dillinger knows his face is everywhere. So he tries to change it.
In late May, he pays for plastic surgery in a Chicago home and uses acid to try to burn off his fingerprints.
It does not work very well. His face is scarred, but still recognisable. And the fingerprints grow back.
He starts living in Chicago under a fake name, Jimmy Lawrence, and dating a waitress named Polly Hamilton.
Polly is staying with a friend, a woman named Ana Cumpanas. In America she goes by Anna Sage.
Anna has a problem of her own. She has run brothels, and the government is trying to deport her to Romania.
She realises who her friend's boyfriend really is. And she sees a way out.
Mid-July. Anna contacts a police sergeant she knows in East Chicago, Martin Zarkovich.
Zarkovich takes her to Melvin Purvis. They meet in a parked car on a Chicago street.
She makes an offer. She will tell them where Dillinger will be. In return, she wants the reward, and help with her deportation.

v.text: I will tell you where he will be.

beats.text: Purvis agrees to put in a word for her. He says he cannot promise more.
Then she gives them the detail that makes the trap possible.
On the night of July 22nd, Dillinger plans to take her and Polly to the movies.
She is not sure which cinema. It will be the Marbro, or the Biograph.
And she will wear orange, so the agents can spot her in the crowd.
Under the theater lights it looks red. The newspapers will call her the Woman in Red.
Sunday, July 22nd, 1934. Chicago is sweltering in a summer heat wave.
Anna calls in the evening. They are going out soon. She still does not know which theater.
Purvis splits his men. Some go to the Marbro. Others wait near the Biograph on Lincoln Avenue.
At the Biograph, a banner promises the theater is cool inside. Air conditioning is still a novelty.
Around half past eight, three people walk up to the ticket booth.
A man in a straw hat and glasses. Polly Hamilton. And a woman in orange.
Purvis sees them. He is sure. It is Dillinger.
The film is Manhattan Melodrama, starring Clark Gable as a gangster who goes to the electric chair.
Purvis calls the Marbro team over. Now every way out is covered.
The plan is simple. When Dillinger walks out, Purvis will light his cigar. That is the signal to close in.
Then they wait. The film runs for more than an hour and a half.
Inside, Dillinger is watching a movie gangster walk calmly to his own execution.
Outside, the theater staff notice strange men hanging around. Someone calls the local police, fearing a robbery.
Officers arrive. Agents have to quietly wave them off before the crowd notices.
At about 10:30, the doors open. The crowd comes out into the heat.
Dillinger walks out between the two women and turns down the sidewalk.
Purvis lights his cigar.
Dillinger seems to sense it. He glances back, and moves toward an alley.
Agents later said he reached for a pistol. Three of them fire.
Dillinger falls at the mouth of the alley. Two women in the crowd are wounded by stray bullets.
He is taken to a nearby hospital, where he is pronounced dead.
Within minutes, a crowd swarms the alley. Some people dip handkerchiefs in the blood on the pavement as souvenirs.
Thousands line up at the Cook County morgue to see the body.
The fingerprints are checked. Despite the acid, they match.
The 141-day manhunt is over. But the story is not.
Anna Sage gets part of the reward, five thousand dollars.
But the deportation goes ahead. In 1936 she is sent back to Romania, where she dies more than a decade later.
Melvin Purvis becomes the most famous lawman in America. Within a year, he leaves the Bureau.
Many believed Hoover resented sharing the spotlight. Purvis said little about it in public.
And the agency that set the trap? In 1935 it gets a new name: the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
The Dillinger case helped turn it from a small office into the most powerful police agency in the country.
One part of the story still starts arguments: what exactly Anna Sage was promised.
She said she was led to believe she could stay in America. Purvis said he had only promised to help.
Either way, the most wanted man in America was not stopped by a fingerprint, a car, or a gunfight in the woods.
He was found because he wanted to see a movie on a hot night, and trusted the wrong friend.
The Biograph Theater still stands on Lincoln Avenue today.
And the alley next to it is exactly where the hunt for Public Enemy Number One ended.
